extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students and general readers of mathematics (topology, elementary analysis)
extracted.subtask_description: Expository textbook material covering elementary topology (fixed-point theorems, genus, Euler characteristic, Jordan curve theorem, five-color theorem, knots) and foundational definitions in functions and complex numbers for readers with undergraduate-level mathematical maturity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the index of boundary transformation vectors
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the index as the algebraic sum of the various changes in angle of the vectors as one traverses the boundary once; clockwise portions are negative, counter-clockwise positive, so the index is an integer (0, ±1, ±2, ...), corresponding to net changes of angle 0, ±360°, ±720°, ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To compute the index, traverse the circle once and add signed angular changes of the transformation vectors; equivalent pictorially by drawing parallel arrows issuing from a single point and counting net revolutions. The convention for sign and the integral-valuedness are essential in subsequent continuity arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Index equals 1 for inward-pointing continuous boundary vectors
rubrics_metrics.description: For a continuous transformation of the disk into itself with no point moved outside the circle and with the transformation vectors on the boundary always directed inside (never tangent), the index of these boundary vectors is 1 (one positive revolution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: the tangent vector makes one complete positive revolution when traversing the circumference; if the transformation vector turned a different integral number of revolutions, it would have to coincide with the tangent (impossible by hypothesis). This fact underpins the fixed-point proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity + integrality implies index constant on concentric circles
rubrics_metrics.description: As one moves from the circumference continuously toward any concentric inner circle, the index of the transformation vectors varies continuously but can take only integral values; thus the index must remain constant (no jumps), so the index on every concentric circle equals its boundary value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle (a quantity continuous in a parameter but taking only integer values is constant) is invoked to reach contradictions on arbitrarily small circles, giving existence conclusions (e.g., fixed points).

rubrics_metrics.name: Brouwer fixed-point theorem for the disk (and homeomorphic regions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any continuous transformation of a disk into itself has at least one fixed point. The theorem also holds for any figure bi-uniquely and continuously correlated with a disk (triangles, squares) and extends to three-dimensional solid spheres (proofs more involved).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofs use the index argument above or equivalent topological obstructions (e.g., impossibility of a continuous retraction of the disk onto its boundary fixing the boundary). This is a standard existence theorem used across topology and dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impossibility of retracting a disk onto its circumference fixing the circumference
rubrics_metrics.description: It is impossible to transform continuously a circular disk into its circumference alone so that each point of the circumference remains fixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalence: a fixed-point-free continuous map of the disk into itself would produce such a retraction (draw arrows from images through original points to boundary), contradicting the impossibility. This impossibility is an alternative statement leading to Brouwer's theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples and exceptions of fixed-point-free continuous transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: Some geometric figures admit continuous fixed-point-free self-transformations: e.g., the annular region between two concentric circles admits rotation by a non-multiple-of-360°; the sphere admits the antipodal map taking each point to its diametrically opposite point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complementary result: any continuous transformation of the sphere that carries no point to its diametrically opposite point (small deformations) must have a fixed point—an analogue to the disk result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topological fixed-point theorems as tools in existence proofs (Poincaré-Birkhoff context)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fixed-point theorems provide powerful methods for proving many mathematical existence theorems not apparently geometrical (e.g., Poincaré's conjecture about periodic orbits in the restricted three-body problem, later proved by Birkhoff).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of topological fixed-point results in dynamical systems yields qualitative existence conclusions such as infinite periodic orbits; historical note on Poincaré and Birkhoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a knot and topological equivalence vs congruence
rubrics_metrics.description: A knot is a closed curve formed by looping and interlacing a string and joining its ends; topologically equivalent knots remain the same under continuous deformations without breaking, but may not be congruent (cannot be rigidly superposed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: mirror-image trefoils are topologically equivalent but not congruent; distinguishing knotted vs unknotted curves and proving non-deformability requires deeper topology and group theory techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of genus of a surface
rubrics_metrics.description: Genus is defined as the largest number of non-intersecting simple closed curves that can be drawn on the surface without separating it; examples: sphere genus 0, torus genus 1, surface with p holes genus p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: the genus is a topological invariant (unchanged by continuous deformation) and characterizes closed surfaces up to deformation (two closed surfaces with same genus are deformable into one another).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification via genus: same genus implies deformability
rubrics_metrics.description: If two closed surfaces have the same genus p, then one may be deformed continuously into the other; the genus p = 0,1,2,... characterizes closed surfaces topologically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: representative models such as sphere with p handles or doughnut with p holes serve as canonical forms for genus p surfaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler characteristic formula for closed two-sided surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: For a closed surface S of genus p, with a subdivision into V vertices, E arcs (edges), and F regions (faces), the relation V - E + F = 2 - 2p holds; the number 2 - 2p is the Euler characteristic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: deform surface to sphere with p handles, cut along joining curves, flatten handles, reduce to sphere minus 2p regions where Euler's formula for the sphere applies. Use this identity in combinatorial/topological arguments (e.g., map coloring).

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler characteristic for one-sided surfaces (including Möbius and cross-cap)
rubrics_metrics.description: For closed one-sided surfaces (e.g., surfaces constructed with cross-caps or Möbius-like identifications) of genus p, the Euler characteristic satisfies V - E + F = 2 - p; notably, a Möbius strip has Euler characteristic 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: cut-and-paste reasoning (cut Möbius strip to a rectangle increases vertices/edges appropriately), or represent one-sided surfaces as sphere with v disks replaced by cross-caps to derive the formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation of surfaces by edge-identified polygons
rubrics_metrics.description: Study of topological surfaces can be simplified by plane polygons with certain pairs of edges conceptually identified (parallel arrows indicating identifications in position and direction), yielding models for closed surfaces and 3D manifolds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Möbius strip and Klein bottle diagrams, cube with identified opposite faces giving three-dimensional torus, and other constructions for visualizing/manipulating manifolds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a regular map and a proper coloring (setup for Five Color Theorem)
rubrics_metrics.description: A map on the sphere is properly colored if no two regions sharing a whole boundary segment receive the same color; consider maps whose regions are bounded by simple closed polygons composed of circular arcs and regular maps where exactly three arcs meet at each vertex (multiple vertices may be regularized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduction: multiple-incident vertices can be replaced by small circles joined to adjacent regions to obtain a regular map without changing the number of regions; proving the five-color theorem is done under the regular-map assumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial identities for regular maps leading to small-face existence
rubrics_metrics.description: For a regular map with F total regions and Fn the number of n-sided regions: F = F2 + F3 + F4 + ... ; also 2E = 3F (each arc has two ends, three arcs end at each vertex) and the vertex-count relation giving via Euler's formula the identity that forces at least one Fi with i < 6 to be positive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From these relations one deduces that at least one face has fewer than six sides; this combinatorial fact is the starting point of the inductive coloring argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five Color Theorem constructive reduction method
rubrics_metrics.description: Proof proceeds by induction: remove a region with ≤4 sides (or perform a specific merge when a 5-sided region has two non-touching neighbors) to obtain a smaller regular map that can be colored with five colors; restore the removed region(s) and choose a color for them using at most five colors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two cases: if an n-sided face has n = 2,3,4 remove an adjacent boundary to reduce regions by one; if n = 5, find two non-touching adjacent regions among its five neighbors, remove two boundaries to reduce by two. Repeat until ≤5 regions remain which are trivially 5-colorable. This yields a constructive though tedious coloring algorithm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jordan curve theorem for polygons via parity (ray counting) method
rubrics_metrics.description: For a simple closed polygon P, classify points p not on P by parity: p is outside (class A) if a ray from p in a fixed direction meets P in an even number of points, and inside (class B) if the number is odd. With specific vertex-counting conventions (do not count a vertex intersection if both incident edges lie on the same side of the ray; count it if they lie on opposite sides), this parity is well-defined and yields two domains separated by P.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show parity is constant along any segment not intersecting P; any polygonal path from A to B must intersect P; construct paths between same-parity points by modifying straight segments via detours along P where needed. This yields a constructive proof of inside/outside classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vertex-counting convention in ray intersections for Jordan theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: When a ray from point p intersects polygon P at a vertex, do not count the intersection if both polygon edges meeting at that vertex lie on the same side of the ray; count it if the two edges lie on opposite sides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This convention ensures parity cannot change spuriously when a moving point's ray passes a vertex, and is essential to the parity-based proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative Jordan curve proof via winding-number (order)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define the order of a point p0 with respect to a closed curve C as the net number of complete revolutions made by an arrow joining p0 to a moving point p on C as p traverses C once; points of even order form the outside, odd order the inside.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This winding-number viewpoint is equivalent to the parity/ray-count method and connects Jordan's theorem to the topological notion of winding number.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental Theorem of Algebra via topological winding-number argument
rubrics_metrics.description: If a complex polynomial f(z) of degree n (>1) had no zero, then for each circle centered at the origin the image curve f(z) avoids 0 and one can define the order (winding number) of 0 with respect to f on that circle; continuity yields ϕ(0)=0 and for large radius ϕ(t)=n, contradiction since ϕ must be integer-valued and continuous, so f has a root.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key analytic estimate: for sufficiently large radius t, the z^n term dominates so f(z) behaves like z^n and winds n times; continuity of f(z) in z implies continuity of the winding number function in t. This topological argument proves existence of at least one complex root.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polar representation and rotation property of z^n (auxiliary for FT of Algebra)
rubrics_metrics.description: If z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), then z^n = r^n (cos nθ + i sin nθ), so as z traverses a circle once, z^n traverses n complete times a circle of radius r^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This trigonometric/polar fact is used to establish that for large radii the image of a circle under the polynomial has winding number n about the origin, underpinning the topological contradiction in the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and conventions for variables and functions
rubrics_metrics.description: A variable ranges arbitrarily over a set S (its domain); a function U = F(X) assigns to each X in S a definite value U in another set T. A continuous variable ranges over an interval of real numbers; independent variable vs dependent variable; constants as special case of functions with singleton range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Domains need not be numeric (can be circles, polygons, finite sets, etc.). Notational and conceptual conventions: use letters from end of alphabet for variables, small letters for numerical continuous variables, and express sequences as functions of integer variable (e.g., a_n = F(n)). The distinction between continuous variable and domain restrictions (e.g., exclude 0 for 1/x) is emphasized.
